text: A correlation ID tells you which log lines belong to the same request, but not how long each step took or which service was actually slow. When Northbridge's checkout latency spikes during a flash sale, you need to know whether it was inventory, payment, or a database call three layers deep. That's distributed tracing, and OpenTelemetry is the standard behind it.

A span is one unit of work — one HTTP call, one query — with a start time, a duration, and attributes describing it. A trace is the full tree of spans handling one request, all sharing a trace ID, with each span's parent_span_id reconstructing exactly which call happened inside which.

OpenTelemetry standardizes three things so you're not locked into one vendor: the APIs and SDKs you instrument your code with, OTLP as the wire protocol for exporting spans, and an optional Collector that routes telemetry to any backend. Instrument once, and send the traces to Jaeger, Tempo, or a commercial vendor just by changing configuration.

Before you can read one trace, you usually have to find it. Jaeger's search page filters by service and minimum duration — exactly how you'd hunt down the slowest checkout requests during a flash sale without already knowing a specific trace ID.

Once you open a trace, you get a waterfall: one bar per span, nested under its parent, sized by duration. In this real trace, a single mysql SELECT under the customer service eats 304 of the 732 total milliseconds — the widest bar is almost always where you look first.
Spans, traces, and a standard way to produce both — that's OpenTelemetry. Next, lesson twenty-three: correlating metrics, logs, and traces together during one live investigation.
